topic: The Mathematics of Fair Sharing: Borsuk-Ulam and the Stolen Necklace
target_audience: Undergraduate students or advanced high school students with an interest in geometry and topology

outline.topic: The Mathematics of Fair Sharing: Borsuk-Ulam and the Stolen Necklace
outline.target_audience: Undergraduate students or advanced high school students with an interest in geometry and topology

sections.title: The Hook: The Thief's Dilemma
sections.content: Introduce two thieves who have stolen a necklace made of different types of precious beads (e.g., rubies and emeralds). They want to split the necklace so that each person gets exactly half of each type of bead. The constraint? They want to make as few cuts as possible to keep the necklace fragments manageable.
sections.example: Visualize a long string with 10 red beads and 8 green beads scattered randomly. The thieves need to find where to snip the string so both get 5 red and 4 green beads.

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Intermediate Value Theorem (1D Logic)
sections.content: Before solving the necklace, we explain the 1D version of the logic. If a continuous path goes from a negative value to a positive value, it must cross zero. This is the foundation for finding 'balance' points.
sections.example: An ant crawling from the bottom of a hill (0m) to the top (10m) must, at some point, be exactly at 5m. There is no way to teleport past the middle.

sections.title: The Borsuk-Ulam Theorem: Antipodal Points
sections.content: Define the theorem visually: On any continuous spherical surface (like Earth), there are always two 'antipodal' points (points directly opposite each other) that share the exact same temperature and barometric pressure simultaneously.
sections.example: Show a 3D globe spinning. If you pick a spot in New York and its exact opposite in the Indian Ocean, the theorem guarantees a pair of such opposite spots exists where the weather gauges match perfectly.

sections.title: Translating the Necklace to Geometry
sections.content: Explain how a necklace can be represented as a mathematical function. We map the distribution of beads along the string to a circle (or a higher-dimensional sphere). A 'cut' is just a way to partition the sphere into two halves.
sections.example: Imagine the necklace wrapped around a transparent ring. A diameter drawn through the ring represents a potential cut. As we rotate this diameter, the amount of 'gold' on each side changes continuously.

sections.title: Solving the Problem: The k-Color Solution
sections.content: Connect the theorem to the necklace: For $k$ types of beads, you need at most $k$ cuts. The Borsuk-Ulam theorem proves that a 'zero point' exists in high-dimensional space where the difference between Thief A's share and Thief B's share is zero for all $k$ types of beads simultaneously.
sections.example: If there are 2 types of beads (Ruby and Sapphire), imagine a 2D map of 'Differences'. The theorem guarantees that at some specific rotation of our cuts, the difference for both rubies and sapphires hits (0,0).

sections.title: Conclusion and Visual Recap
sections.content: Summarize that topology—the math of shapes and continuity—can solve discrete problems of fairness. Reiterate that even if we don't know *where* to cut, math proves a fair cut *must* exist.
sections.example: An animation of the two thieves happily walking away with two different piles of beads that are perfectly equal in value and type, thanks to the 'invisible hand' of the Borsuk-Ulam theorem.

storyboard.title: The Hook: The Thief's Dilemma
lecture_lines: Two thieves stole a necklace of rubies and emeralds.
They must share the beads perfectly in half.
What is the minimum number of cuts required?
animations: Create a horizontal line (the necklace) with 6 rubies [Asset: /mmfs1/data/home/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/ruby.svg] and 4 emeralds [Asset: /mmfs1/data/home/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/emerald.svg] placed randomly.
Split the screen into two zones labeled 'Thief A' and 'Thief B' in #FFFFFF.

Display a target text 'Goal: 3 Rubies [Asset: /mmfs1/data/home/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/ruby.svg], 2 Emeralds [Asset: /mmfs1/data/home/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/emerald.svg]' in the center with a yellow highlight (#FFFF00).
Show a dashed vertical line (#FFFFFF) moving along the necklace to represent a single cut.

storyboard.title: Prerequisite: The Intermediate Value Theorem (1D Logic)
lecture_lines: An ant crawls from a valley to a peak.
It must pass every height in between the two.
This continuous path ensures a middle point exists.
animations: Draw a smooth hill curve (#8B4513) from bottom-left to top-right.
Animate a small blue circle (#0000FF) as the ant moving from the start to the peak.
Draw a dashed horizontal line at the hill's midpoint (#FFD700) and highlight the intersection point with the ant's path.

storyboard.title: The Borsuk-Ulam Theorem: Antipodal Points
lecture_lines: Imagine two opposite points on the Earth's surface.
These are called antipodal points on a sphere.
Borsuk-Ulam says two opposite points share identical weather.
Temperature and pressure match at these two locations.
A continuous mapping always finds this balanced pair.
animations: Display a 2D blue circle representing Earth (#0000FF) with weather labels 'T' and 'P' scattered on it.
Draw a diameter line through the center, highlighting the two endpoints in #FF0000.
Animate the 'T' and 'P' values at these endpoints changing until they are exactly equal.
Flash the labels 'Antipodal Balance' at the matching points in #00FF00.

storyboard.title: Translating the Necklace to Geometry
lecture_lines: Wrap the necklace around a transparent circular ring.
A single diameter represents a cut across the loop.
Rotating this diameter changes the bead counts continuously.
animations: Bend the straight necklace from section 1 into a circular ring with the same rubies and emeralds.
Add a white diameter line (#FFFFFF) that can rotate around the center point.
Show numbers for 'Side A' and 'Side B' rubies/emeralds updating as the diameter rotates.

storyboard.title: Solving the Problem: The k-Color Solution
lecture_lines: For two bead types, two cuts are always enough.
The theorem finds where bead differences are zero.
This logic extends to any number of bead varieties.
For k types, k cuts guarantee a fair split.
Topology proves a perfect solution always exists.
animations: Show the necklace ring with the rotating diameter representing two cuts.
Draw a 2D vector (x, y) starting from the center, where x is ruby difference and y is emerald difference.
Animate the vector tip moving towards the origin (0, 0) as the diameter rotates to the correct position.
Highlight the final cut positions on the necklace ring in gold (#FFD700).

storyboard.title: Conclusion and Visual Recap
lecture_lines: Topology ensures fairness through continuous geometric shapes.
Math proves the solution exists before we find it.
The thieves can now share their loot perfectly.
animations: Show the necklace from section 1 split into two identical piles of beads ([Asset: /mmfs1/data/home/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/ruby.svg] and [Asset: /mmfs1/data/home/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/emerald.svg]).
Display the word 'TOPOLOGY' in large letters with a glow effect (#00FFFF).
Fade to a final scene with the two thieves (labels 'A' and 'B') and a 'Fair Split' checkmark (#00FF00).
